The largest release this project has had, and the first one that breaks
something.  A native compiler through LLVM arrived; the compiled file format
left; and both are described below in the order they matter.

**Upgrading from 3.4.x: a `.scmc` file no longer runs, and `goscheme build` is
now `goscheme pack`.**  Nothing else changes — your `.scm` files are untouched,
and a packed program still runs anywhere the interpreter runs.  If a script of
yours calls `goscheme build`, repoint it at `goscheme pack`.  Why this was worth
breaking is argued in [docs/open-source.md](../docs/open-source.md); the short
version is that the thing removed was not load-bearing.

### `goscheme compile` produces a native executable

A program can now be compiled to machine code through LLVM — `opt`, `llc` and a
C compiler — instead of to a stored bytecode file:

```sh
goscheme compile program.scm -o program
goscheme compile program.scm -S          # emit the LLVM IR and stop
goscheme compile program.scm -static     # link the runtime in, ~8 MB
```

It is a **hybrid**, and the honest way to describe it is that it compiles a
subset.  A procedure whose body is a computation over its parameters, constants
and globals becomes machine code; everything else — macros, `call/cc`, the
library, anything the compiler cannot prove — goes to the runtime, which is the
interpreter linked into the binary.  So the speedup depends entirely on how much
of a program falls inside that subset.

Measured on the twelve benchmarks, compiled against the interpreter:

| | |
|---|---|
| `tail-loop` | 4.2× |
| `fib` | 4.1× |
| `locals` | 2.6× |
| `lists`, `sort`, `globals`, `higher-order` | 1.2 – 1.4× |
| `strings`, `mini-eval`, `closures`, `vectors` | ~1.0× |

And against C doing the same work, with C's whole-loop rewrites held back:
**42× slower**, where the interpreter is 73×.  Compiling closes a little over
half the distance, and the four rows within an order of magnitude —
`tail-loop` 8.3×, `vectors` 9.3×, `lists` 11.4×, `locals` 14.5× — are the four
whose inner loop is recognised and run as a single call into the runtime.

The far end is not slow machine code but programs with little machine code in
them: `strings` and `mini-eval` compile *nothing at all*, so every call they
make crosses into the interpreter, and a crossing costs about 138 ns however
little work is on the other side.  That is the design, not a defect, and
[docs/compile.md](../docs/compile.md) says what it accepts and what it refuses.

A compiled program is **about 16 KB** by default: the runtime is a shared library
and several programs on one machine share one copy of the interpreter.
`-static` links it in for a program that has to run where the library is not
installed.

### The compiled file format is gone

`.scmc` — a bytecode file with a version, a symbol table and an obfuscation pass
— has been removed, along with `goscheme build` and the obfuscation it existed to
provide.

The reasoning is that a `.scmc` was a *second* thing to keep, version and explain
in exchange for a saving nobody could measure: compiling a script takes
milliseconds, so the stored form bought no speed.  What replaces it is
`goscheme pack`, which takes the comments and the layout out of the source and
leaves the source.  A packed program is still readable Scheme, which is the point
— see [docs/open-source.md](../docs/open-source.md) for why that matters more
than the bytes.

### The compiler got a memory model

Two bugs of the same shape, both found by asking why a loop that computes one
number was slow:

- A **literal was built where it was written**, not once.  `"hello"` in a loop
  meant reading the source text back, parsing it and allocating a fresh string
  *per iteration*.  Constants are now built once, in `main`, into module-level
  storage.
- The **call cache was a stack slot**, so a loop written as tail recursion
  cleared it on every entry and re-resolved the name every iteration — and
  because the runtime caches a resolved procedure by storing it in an
  append-only table, each iteration left an entry nothing could reclaim.  300000
  iterations left 300002 entries; the loop now leaves 3.

### Mutual recursion, and a forward `letrec*`

Two shapes the compiler used to refuse, both because a rule was reasoned about
rather than measured:

- **Mutual recursion** was dropped on the premise that "LLVM will not accept
  either ordering".  It will: a forward reference to a function in the same
  module resolves, and the topological order the generator walks was its own
  bookkeeping.  `even2?`/`odd2?` — two tail calls to each other — now run
  5,000,000 deep in constant stack, **196× faster than interpreted**.
- **A `letrec*` that refers forward** was refused, correctly: it used to be
  rewritten into a `let*`, which is wrong for that shape and wrong in a way that
  crashed.  The fix was to give the form its real meaning — every binding gets a
  heap cell before any initialiser runs, so a lambda captures the *location* of a
  name bound later.  The R7RS suite's `means` now agrees with the interpreter.

### What is still not compiled

`call/cc`, `raise`, `dynamic-wind` and `guard` are refused, and a body that
mentions one runs in the interpreter.  A compiled frame has no continuation to
return into, so control cannot be unwound through it.  The mechanism that solves
this is known — LLVM's SJLJ exception handling, with a landing pad per frame —
and a version of it was built and withdrawn: it works across one compiled frame
and loses the handler's value across three.  [docs/compiler-notes.md](../docs/compiler-notes.md)
records what was learned and what finishing it would take.

### Smaller things

- `goscheme compile` refuses fewer things, and says why when it does.  A
  procedure declined for speed is reported as declined, not as a defect.
- A named let whose body is not a walk, and an `arith.fast` block emitted after a
  terminator, were two bugs reachable only through `-compile-all`; both are fixed.
- The REPL and the CLI are unchanged in behaviour.

### Verification

The standard used throughout is **comparing the two engines' output** on every
benchmark under both the default path and `-compile-all`, plus 2568 assertions
across eleven Scheme suites and four Go packages.  [docs/compiler-notes.md](../docs/compiler-notes.md)
also records three measurement mistakes made while doing this, because they all
had the same shape and the next one will too.
